benchmarks.title: Benchmark results
benchmarks.description: Single-thread numbers measured on Apple Silicon (M-series).
benchmarks.chart_note: * About 600x faster, so rule execution barely shows up in request latency.
benchmarks.modes_desc: The same rules can run in four ways. Pick the one that fits the workload.
benchmarks.mode_treewalk_desc: Interprets the AST directly. Good for development and one-off rules.
benchmarks.mode_vm_desc: Compiles rules to bytecode. The default in production.
benchmarks.mode_vectorized_desc: Processes inputs column by column in batches, for validating large datasets.
benchmarks.mode_jit_desc: Compiles to native machine code, with latency in nanoseconds.
benchmarks.jit_desc: Compiles numeric rules to native machine code with Cranelift. 20–30x faster than the bytecode VM on compute-heavy rules.

integration.title: Integration
integration.desc: Run Ordo as a service, in the browser, or as a library inside a Rust program.
integration.deploy_desc: Pick the option that matches how you deploy.
integration.invoke_desc: Standard protocols with existing clients in most languages.
integration.method_cloud_desc: Deploy via Docker/K8s/Nomad, serving rules via HTTP/gRPC.
integration.method_edge_desc: Runs in the browser or on edge nodes via WASM, with no network call.
integration.method_embedded_desc: Compiled into your Rust application as a library, with no network or serialization cost.

syntax.title: Expression Syntax
syntax.desc: C-like syntax with the usual operators and a set of built-in functions.

roadmap.title: Roadmap
roadmap.desc: Ordo started as a fast rule engine. The direction now is a business rule layer: people or AI write the rules, and Ordo tests them and shows what a change affects.
